title: Victims of crime, bail and the civil side of criminal matters

items.title: Criminal Code: who is a victim
items.says: The Criminal Code defines a victim as a person against whom an offence was committed or is said to have been committed, and who suffered (or is said to have suffered) physical or emotional harm, property damage or economic loss because of it.

source.expect: who has suffered, or is alleged to have suffered

review.problem: Section 2 only defines 'victim'; it does not say the Code sets out crimes, bail, peace bonds, trials and sentencing.

items.title: Canadian Victims Bill of Rights
items.says: The Canadian Victims Bill of Rights defines a victim as an individual who suffered physical or emotional harm, property damage or economic loss as the result of an offence or alleged offence.

source.expect: property damage or economic loss as the result

review.problem: Section 2 only defines 'victim'; the list of rights to information, protection, participation and restitution is not in it.

items.title: Ontario Victims' Bill of Rights, 1995
items.says: Under Ontario's Victims' Bill of Rights, 1995, a victim is a person who suffers emotional or physical harm, property loss or damage, or economic harm because of a crime by another. If the crime causes death, it includes the person's child, parent, dependant or spouse, but not one who is charged with or convicted of the crime.

source.expect: suffers emotional or physical harm, loss of or damage

review.problem: Section 1 only defines 'victim' and 'crime'; principles for officials (s. 2) and civil-lawsuit rules are not in it, and the exclusion of family members charged with the crime is dropped.

items.title: Crown Attorneys Act
items.says: No one may be appointed as, or act as, a Crown Attorney or assistant Crown Attorney unless they are a member of the bar of Ontario.

source.expect: who is not a member of the bar of Ontario

review.problem: Section 4 only sets the qualification; it does not create the offices or set out their duties.

items.title: Ministry of the Attorney General Act
items.says: The Attorney General oversees all matters connected with the administration of justice in Ontario, and conducts litigation for and against the Crown.

source.expect: superintend all matters connected with the administration of justice

items.title: Limitations Act, 2002
items.says: Unless the Limitations Act, 2002 provides otherwise, a court case about a claim cannot be started after the second anniversary of the day the claim was discovered.

source.expect: after the second anniversary of the day on which the claim was discovered

review.problem: Section 4 sets only the basic two-year period; the statement that some sexual assault or assault claims have no deadline is not in s. 4 (it is elsewhere in the Act).

items.title: Reporting the offence to police
items.says: Under the Canadian Victims Bill of Rights, once an offence is reported to the appropriate authorities in the criminal justice system, the investigation is treated as having begun at the time of the report, and the victim's rights under that Act apply while it is investigated or prosecuted.

source.expect: the investigation of the offence is deemed to begin at the time of the reporting

review.problem: s. 18 (2) does not say a criminal matter usually starts with a report to police; it speaks of a report to 'the appropriate authorities in the criminal justice system' and deems the investigation to begin then.

items.title: Laying a private information
items.says: Any person who believes on reasonable grounds that someone has committed an indictable offence may lay an information (a sworn written charge) before a justice of the peace. The justice must receive it.

source.expect: may lay an information in writing and under oath before a justice

items.title: Hearing before a charge laid by a private person goes ahead
items.says: When a private person lays an information, a judge or designated justice holds a hearing in private, without the accused, to hear the person's allegations and witnesses. A summons or warrant can issue only if the Attorney General got a copy of the information, reasonable notice, and an opportunity to attend, cross-examine and call evidence.

source.expect: has heard and considered, ex parte and in camera

items.title: Crown can take over a private prosecution
items.says: A Crown Attorney watches over cases run by private prosecutors. The Crown is not to interfere unnecessarily, but takes over the whole case where justice towards the accused seems to require it.

source.expect: watch over cases conducted by private prosecutors

items.title: Crown stay of proceedings
items.says: The Attorney General, or a Crown counsel instructed for that purpose, may stay a criminal proceeding at any time after it starts and before judgment. A stayed proceeding can be restarted by notice, but if no notice is given within one year, or before the time for starting the proceeding would have run out if that is earlier, it is treated as never having been started.

source.expect: the proceedings are stayed by the Attorney General

review.problem: Drops the condition that a stayed proceeding is also treated as never started if no notice is given before the time for starting it would have run out, whichever is earlier than one year.

items.title: Crown charge screening
items.says: Ontario Crown prosecutors review each charge to decide whether the prosecution continues. The Crown Prosecution Manual sets out the screening standard the Crown applies, which includes whether there is a reasonable prospect of conviction and whether the prosecution is in the public interest.

source.citation: Ministry of the Attorney General, Crown Prosecution Manual, Directive: Charge Screening
source.expect: reasonable prospect of conviction

items.title: Right to respect, courtesy, compassion and fairness
items.says: Every victim has the right to be treated with respect, courtesy, compassion and fairness by the authorities in the criminal justice system.

source.expect: treated with respect, courtesy, compassion and fairness

items.title: Interest in a timely trial
items.says: Every victim has the right to have their interest in a timely trial, and in the timely resolution of matters relating to the offence, taken into consideration.

source.expect: their interest in a timely trial

items.title: Right to general information
items.says: Every victim has the right to information about the criminal justice system and their role in it, the services and programs available to them, their right to complain, and their rights under the Act.

source.expect: the criminal justice system and the role of victims in it

items.title: Right to information about the investigation and court dates
items.says: Every victim has the right to information about the status and outcome of the investigation, and about where and when court proceedings take place, their progress and their outcome.

source.expect: the status and outcome of the investigation into the offence

items.title: Right to information about protection measures
items.says: Every victim has the right to information about the protection measures available to them in the criminal justice system.

source.expect: information about the protection measures available to them

items.title: Right to information about restorative justice
items.says: Every victim has the right to information about available restorative justice processes, how they work, and that taking part is voluntary at every stage. If the victim and the accused or offender take part, the victim has the right to information about whether the agreed terms were carried out.

source.expect: the voluntary nature of participation at every stage

items.title: Right to information about the offender's release
items.says: Every victim has the right to information about conditional release reviews of the offender and the timing and conditions of release, and, if the accused is found not criminally responsible or unfit to stand trial, about the hearings held to make dispositions for the accused and the dispositions made.

source.expect: the timing and conditions of that release

review.problem: Section 8(b) speaks of hearings held to make dispositions (and the dispositions made), not specifically Review Board hearings.

items.title: Right to have security considered
items.says: Every victim has the right to have their security considered by the authorities in the criminal justice system.

source.expect: have their security considered

items.title: Protection from intimidation and retaliation
items.says: Every victim has the right to have reasonable and necessary measures taken to protect them from intimidation and retaliation.

source.expect: protect the victim from intimidation and retaliation

items.title: Right to have privacy considered
items.says: Every victim has the right to have their privacy considered by the authorities in the criminal justice system.

source.expect: have their privacy considered

items.title: Identity protection
items.says: A victim who is a complainant or witness has the right to be asked whether they want their identity protected, to request protection, to be told when an order is made, and to be told of their right to apply to revoke or vary it.

source.expect: be asked whether they wish to have their identity protected

items.title: Right to request testimonial aids
items.says: Every victim has the right to request testimonial aids when appearing as a witness.

source.expect: the right to request testimonial aids

items.title: Right to have views considered
items.says: Every victim has the right to convey their views about decisions by authorities that affect their rights under the Act, and to have those views considered.

source.expect: convey their views about decisions to be made

items.title: Right to present a victim impact statement
items.says: Every victim has the right to present a victim impact statement to the court, and a victim statement to other authorities such as the Correctional Service of Canada and the Parole Board of Canada, and to have it considered.

source.expect: present a victim impact statement to the court

items.title: Right to have restitution considered
items.says: Every victim has the right to have the court consider making a restitution order against the offender.

source.expect: consider making a restitution order against the offender

items.title: Right to enforce restitution as a civil judgment
items.says: A victim who is owed money under a restitution order and is not paid has the right to have the order entered as a civil court judgment that can be enforced against the offender.

source.expect: entered as a civil court judgment

items.title: Who may act for a victim
items.says: If the victim has died or cannot act for themselves, their rights may be exercised by a spouse, a person who lived with them in a conjugal relationship for at least one year, a relative or dependant, or a person who has custody of or cares for the victim or the victim's dependant.

source.expect: if the victim is dead or incapable of acting on their own behalf

items.title: Accused persons are not victims under the Act
items.says: A person charged with, found guilty of, or found not criminally responsible or unfit for the offence is not a victim of that offence under the Act.

source.expect: if the individual is charged with the offence

items.title: When the rights apply
items.says: The Act applies while the offence is investigated or prosecuted, while the offender is in the corrections or conditional release process, and while an accused found not criminally responsible or unfit is under a court or Review Board.

source.expect: while the offence is investigated or prosecuted

items.title: Rights are exercised through existing legal mechanisms
items.says: Victims exercise their rights under the Act through the mechanisms the law already provides. A victim can exercise these rights only if they are in Canada or are a Canadian citizen or permanent resident.

source.expect: exercised through the mechanisms provided by law

review.problem: Section 19(1) says only that rights are exercised through the mechanisms provided by law; the rule about not interfering with police or prosecutorial discretion or causing delay is in s. 20, a different section.

items.title: Limits on how the Act is applied
items.says: The Act is applied in a way that is reasonable and that does not interfere with the proper administration of justice, police discretion, prosecutorial discretion, or anyone's safety.

source.expect: causing interference with prosecutorial discretion

items.title: No party status in the criminal case
items.says: The Act does not make a victim a party, intervenor or observer in a criminal proceeding, and does not take that status away where the law otherwise gives it.

source.expect: the status of party, intervenor or observer in any proceedings

items.title: No lawsuit for breach of the Act
items.says: No cause of action or right to damages arises from an infringement or denial of a right under the Canadian Victims Bill of Rights.

source.expect: No cause of action or right to damages arises

items.title: No appeal only because a victim's right was denied
items.says: No appeal lies from a decision or order solely because a right under the Act was infringed or denied.

source.expect: No appeal lies from any decision or order solely

items.title: Complaint to a federal body
items.says: A victim who believes a federal department, agency or body denied their rights may complain through that body's complaints mechanism. If not satisfied after using it, they may complain to any authority that reviews complaints about that body.

source.expect: has the right to file a complaint in accordance with its complaints mechanism

review.problem: s. 25 names no bodies; the examples (RCMP, Public Prosecution Service of Canada, Correctional Service of Canada, Parole Board) are added.

items.title: Further complaint after the federal process
items.says: A victim who has used up a federal body's complaints process and is not satisfied may file a complaint with an authority that has jurisdiction to review complaints about that body. The body's process must review the complaint, can make recommendations, and must tell the victim the result.

source.expect: who has exhausted their recourse under the complaints mechanism

items.title: Complaint about an Ontario body
items.says: A victim who believes a provincial department, agency or body denied their rights under the Act may complain in accordance with the laws of the province.

source.expect: may file a complaint in accordance with the laws of the province

review.problem: s. 26 names no examples; 'a police service or a Crown Attorney's office' is added, and a municipal police service is not obviously a 'provincial or territorial department, agency or body'.

items.title: Ontario principle: courtesy, compassion and respect
items.says: Ontario's Victims' Bill of Rights sets out as a principle that justice system officials treat victims with courtesy, compassion and respect for their personal dignity and privacy.

source.expect: respect for their personal dignity and privacy

items.title: Ontario principle: access to information
items.says: Under Ontario's principles, victims have access to information about services and remedies, the progress of the investigation, the charges laid (or why none were laid), court dates and outcomes, any plea arrangements, the accused's interim release and sentencing, and their right to make a victim impact statement.

source.expect: the reasons why no charges are laid

items.title: Ontario principle: notice of release or escape
items.says: A victim of a prescribed crime who asks is to be notified of any application for release or upcoming release of the convicted person, including temporary absence or parole, and of any escape from custody.

source.expect: any escape of the convicted person from custody

items.title: Ontario principle: sexual assault interviews
items.says: A victim of sexual assault who asks is to be interviewed during the investigation only by police officers and officials of the same gender as the victim.

source.expect: only by police officers and officials of the same gender

items.title: Ontario principle: return of property
items.says: A victim's property held by justice officials is to be returned promptly once it is no longer needed for the justice system.

source.expect: should be returned promptly to the victim

items.title: Limits on the Ontario principles
items.says: The Ontario principles are subject to available resources and information, what is reasonable in the case, what is consistent with the law and the public interest, and what is needed so that criminal proceedings are not delayed.

source.expect: subject to the availability of resources and information

items.title: No new legal remedy from the Ontario principles
items.says: The principles in section 2 do not create any new cause of action, right of appeal, claim or other remedy.

source.expect: No new cause of action, right of appeal, claim or other remedy

items.title: Victims' Justice Fund
items.says: Ontario keeps a victims' justice fund account, funded in part by fine surcharges, and the money is used to assist victims, including by supporting programs and community agencies.

source.expect: shall be used to assist victims

items.title: Office for Victims of Crime
items.says: The Office for Victims of Crime advises the Attorney General on how the victims' principles are respected, on standards for victim services, and on the use of the Victims' Justice Fund.

source.expect: ways to ensure that the principles set out in subsection 2 (1)

items.title: Bail (judicial interim release) hearing
items.says: When an accused is brought before a justice (other than for murder and the other offences listed in s. 469), the justice must release them without conditions unless the prosecutor shows cause why detention, or a release with conditions, is justified.

source.expect: make a release order in respect of that offence, without conditions

items.title: Release at the earliest opportunity, on the least onerous conditions
items.says: Police, justices and judges give primary consideration to releasing the accused at the earliest reasonable opportunity, on the least onerous conditions that are appropriate, including conditions the accused can reasonably comply with, while taking the grounds for detention into account.

source.expect: at the earliest reasonable opportunity and on the least onerous conditions

review.problem: The last sentence (does not require release; does not apply in a reverse-onus situation) comes from s. 493.11, a separate section, not s. 493.1.

items.title: Release is not required; conditions must address the risks
items.says: A justice or judge who releases the accused imposes the least onerous conditions needed to address the risks under the detention grounds, including public safety, and does not release the accused if detention is justified.

source.expect: shall not order that the accused be released if the detention of the accused is justified

items.title: Particular attention to Indigenous and vulnerable accused
items.says: In bail decisions, police, justices and judges give particular attention to the circumstances of Indigenous accused and of accused from vulnerable populations who are overrepresented in the justice system.

source.expect: give particular attention to the circumstances of

items.title: Release order with conditions
items.says: If release without conditions is not ordered, the justice makes a release order with conditions, unless the prosecutor shows detention is justified. The order may add a promise to pay, sureties, or a cash deposit.

source.expect: make a release order that sets out the conditions directed by the justice

items.title: The ladder: least onerous form of release
items.says: A justice cannot order a more onerous form of release (promise to pay, sureties, deposit) unless the prosecution shows why each less onerous form would be inadequate. This rule does not apply to a reverse-onus accused.

source.expect: for any less onerous form of release would be inadequate

items.title: Sureties
items.says: Before a particular person is named as a surety, they give the judge or justice a signed sworn or solemn declaration (Form 12) setting out, among other things, their contact information, suitability including finances, relationship to the accused, the amount they are willing to promise or deposit, and that they understand and voluntarily accept a surety's role.

source.expect: signed declaration under oath, solemn declaration or solemn affirmation in Form 12

review.problem: The rule that a surety must be the least onerous form of release is in s. 515(2.03), not s. 515.1(1), which deals only with the surety's declaration.

items.title: Factors: intimate partner violence and record
items.says: In making a bail order the justice considers relevant factors, including whether the offence charged involved violence used, threatened or attempted against the accused's intimate partner, random and unprovoked violence, and any previous criminal convictions, including ones involving violence.

source.expect: violence was used, threatened or attempted against their intimate partner

review.problem: Section 515(3) does not define 'intimate partner'; that definition is in s. 2.

items.title: Conditions that protect a victim
items.says: A release order can require the accused to report to police, stay in an area, not communicate directly or indirectly with any victim or witness named in the order, stay away from named places, give up passports, and follow other conditions needed for the safety and security of any victim or witness.

source.expect: abstain from communicating, directly or indirectly, with any victim, witness or other person

items.title: Weapons prohibition on release
items.says: For certain offences, including those involving violence against a person, the justice must add a condition banning firearms and other weapons, and must give reasons if this condition is not added.

source.expect: shall add to the order a condition prohibiting the accused from possessing a firearm

items.title: Considering extra safety conditions
items.says: For certain offences, including violent offences (among them violence against an intimate partner), the justice must consider whether to add no-contact, stay-away or other conditions in the interest of the safety and security of any person, particularly a victim or witness, and, if the Attorney General asks, a condition that the accused wear an electronic monitoring device.

source.expect: particularly a victim of or witness to the offence

review.problem: Drops the condition that an electronic monitoring device is considered only if the Attorney General asks for it.

items.title: Reverse onus: when the accused must show why release is justified
items.says: For certain charges, the justice orders detention unless the accused shows cause why detention is not justified, by clearly demonstrating that their release plan addresses the risks under the detention grounds. These include indictable offences said to be committed while already on release, certain firearm and organized-crime offences, choking or strangulation in an assault or sexual assault, and breach-of-bail charges said to be committed while on release.

source.expect: clearly demonstrating that their proposed release plan addresses the risks

items.title: Reverse onus: intimate partner violence with a prior record
items.says: The accused bears the onus where they are charged with an offence involving violence against an intimate partner and they were previously convicted of violence against an intimate partner, or were bound by a peace bond laid on behalf of an intimate partner at the time.

source.expect: violence was allegedly used, threatened or attempted against their intimate partner

items.title: Ground 1: attendance in court
items.says: Detention is justified only on one or more of three grounds. The first is where detention is necessary to make sure the accused attends court.

source.expect: necessary to ensure his or her attendance in court

items.title: Ground 2: protection or safety of the public, including the victim
items.says: The second ground is where detention is necessary for the protection or safety of the public, including any victim or witness or anyone under 18, having regard to any substantial likelihood that the accused will commit an offence or interfere with the administration of justice if released.

source.expect: including any victim of or witness to the offence

items.title: Ground 3: confidence in the administration of justice
items.says: The third ground is where detention is necessary to maintain confidence in the administration of justice, looking at all the circumstances including the apparent strength of the prosecution's case, the gravity of the offence, how it was committed (including firearm use), the possible length of imprisonment, and outstanding charges.

source.expect: necessary to maintain confidence in the administration of justice

items.title: Detention order
items.says: If the prosecutor shows cause for detention, the justice orders the accused detained until dealt with according to law and records reasons.

source.expect: the justice shall order that the accused be detained in custody

items.title: No-contact order while detained
items.says: A justice who orders an accused detained may include a direction that they not communicate, directly or indirectly, with any victim, witness or other person named in the order, except under any conditions the justice sets.

source.expect: may include in the order a direction that the accused abstain from communicating

review.problem: Section 515(12) does not say that breaking the no-contact direction is an offence.

items.title: Victim safety must be considered on the record
items.says: A justice making any bail order must state on the record that they considered the safety and security of every victim of the offence and of the community.

source.expect: considered the safety and security of every victim of the offence

items.title: Victim may request a copy of the bail order
items.says: If a victim asks, the justice must have a copy of the bail order given to the victim. When releasing an accused with conditions, the justice must ask the prosecutor whether victims were told of this right.

source.expect: cause a copy of the order to be given to the victim

items.title: Court asks whether victims were told
items.says: On making a release order with conditions, the justice must ask the prosecutor whether victims have been informed of their right to request a copy of the order.

source.expect: whether victims of the offence have been informed of their right to request a copy

items.title: Bail hearing adjournment limit
items.says: A bail hearing can be adjourned on application, but not for more than three clear days without the accused's consent.

source.expect: no adjournment shall be for more than three clear days

items.title: Publication ban on bail evidence
items.says: The justice may, and must if the accused applies, ban publication of the evidence, information, representations and reasons at the bail hearing until the accused is discharged at a preliminary inquiry or the trial ends.

source.expect: shall on application by the accused

items.title: Evidence about victim safety at the bail hearing
items.says: At a bail hearing, the justice must take into consideration any evidence submitted about the need to ensure the safety or security of any victim or witness. The prosecutor may lead evidence of the accused's record, outstanding charges, past breaches and the circumstances of the offence.

source.expect: the need to ensure the safety or security of any victim of or witness

items.title: No-contact condition takes effect immediately
items.says: A no-contact condition with a victim or witness in a release order takes effect from the moment it is made, whether or not the accused has yet left custody.

source.expect: is effective from the moment it is made

items.title: Changing a release order by consent
items.says: A release order can be varied with the written consent of the accused, the prosecutor and any sureties. The varied order is treated as a release order under section 515.

source.expect: may be varied with the written consent of the accused, prosecutor and any sureties

review.problem: Section 519.1 says nothing about a victim raising a change with the Crown or not being able to consent.

items.title: Bail review by the accused
items.says: An accused may apply to a judge, at any time before trial, to review a release or detention order.

source.expect: apply to a judge for a review of the order

items.title: Bail review by the prosecutor
items.says: The prosecutor may apply to a judge, at any time before trial, to review a release order (or a no-contact direction in a detention order).

source.expect: the prosecutor may, at any time before the trial of the charge

review.problem: Section 521(1) says nothing about a victim asking the Crown or being unable to bring a review.

items.title: Notice of bail review
items.says: An accused's bail review is not heard unless the accused gave the prosecutor at least two clear days' written notice, unless the prosecutor consents otherwise.

source.expect: at least two clear days notice in writing

review.problem: Section 520(2) covers only an accused's review (notice to the prosecutor); notice on a prosecutor's review is in s. 521(2), a different section.

items.title: What the review judge considers
items.says: On review, the judge may consider the transcript, exhibits and new evidence, and either dismisses the application or, if the applicant shows cause, vacates or varies the order.

source.expect: dismiss the application

items.title: 30-day bar on repeat reviews
items.says: After a bail review is heard, no further review may be brought for the same accused within 30 days of the decision without a judge's leave.

source.expect: before the expiry of 30 days from the date of the decision

items.title: Bail review procedure in the Superior Court
items.says: Bail reviews are heard in the Superior Court of Justice under the Criminal Proceedings Rules for that court, which set out the application materials and filing requirements.

source.citation: Criminal Proceedings Rules for the Superior Court of Justice (Ontario), SI/2012-7
source.expect: judicial interim release

items.title: Bail for murder and other s. 469 offences
items.says: For murder and other offences listed in s. 469, only a Superior Court judge can release the accused, and the accused must show why detention is not justified. The judge may add a no-contact direction to a detention order.

source.expect: shall order that the accused be detained in custody unless the accused

items.title: Breaching a release order is an offence
items.says: An accused who, without lawful excuse, fails to comply with a condition of a release order, or with a no-contact order made on detention, commits an offence punishable by up to two years.

source.expect: fails, without lawful excuse, to comply with a condition of that release order

items.title: Cancelling release after a breach or new offence
items.says: When an accused is arrested for breaching a release order or for a new offence while on release, the justice cancels the order if satisfied the accused breached it or there are reasonable grounds to believe they committed an offence.

source.expect: shall cancel a summons, appearance notice, undertaking or release order

items.title: After cancellation, the accused bears the onus
items.says: If the release order is cancelled, in the listed circumstances the accused is detained unless they show cause why detention is not justified.

source.expect: order that the accused be detained in custody unless the accused

items.title: 90-day detention review
items.says: If an accused is still detained awaiting trial 90 days after first appearing (or after a detention or review decision), the jailer must apply to a judge to fix a hearing on whether continued detention is justified.

source.expect: immediately after the expiry of those 90 days

items.title: Peace bond (s. 810 recognizance): laying the information
items.says: Any person who fears on reasonable grounds that another person will injure them, their intimate partner or child, or damage their property, or will commit the offence of sharing an intimate image without consent (s. 162.1), may lay an information before a justice, or have one laid on their behalf.

source.expect: fears on reasonable grounds that another person

review.problem: Section 810(1) does not say that no criminal charge is needed.

items.title: Parties appear before the court
items.says: A justice who receives a peace bond information must have both parties appear before a justice or summary conviction court.

source.expect: shall cause the parties to appear before him

items.title: Crown or private conduct of a peace bond
items.says: Every Crown Attorney and every provincial prosecutor is the agent of the Attorney General for the purposes of the Criminal Code.

source.expect: is the agent of the Attorney General for the purposes of the Criminal Code

review.problem: Section 10 says only that Crown Attorneys and provincial prosecutors are the Attorney General's agents for the Criminal Code; it says nothing about peace bond hearings, the informant conducting them, or peace bonds resolving charges.

items.title: Test: reasonable grounds for the fear
items.says: If the court is satisfied by the evidence that the person has reasonable grounds for the fear, it may order the defendant to enter into a recognizance to keep the peace and be of good behaviour for up to 12 months.

source.expect: has reasonable grounds for the fear

items.title: Refusing to enter the peace bond
items.says: A defendant who fails or refuses to enter into the ordered recognizance may be committed to prison for up to 12 months.

source.expect: fails or refuses to enter into the recognizance

items.title: Conditions in a peace bond
items.says: The court may add any reasonable conditions it considers desirable to secure the defendant's good conduct, including abstaining from drugs or alcohol.

source.expect: any reasonable conditions to the recognizance

items.title: Weapons condition in a peace bond
items.says: Before ordering a peace bond, the court must consider whether to ban the defendant from possessing firearms and other weapons, and must give reasons if it does not.

source.expect: prohibited from possessing any firearm

items.title: No-contact and stay-away conditions
items.says: The court must consider whether, for the safety of the person who laid the information or their intimate partner or child, to bar the defendant from places where they are regularly found and from communicating with them.

source.expect: prohibiting the defendant from communicating, in whole or in part

items.title: Changing peace bond conditions
items.says: Either the informant or the defendant may apply to the court to vary the conditions of the recognizance.

source.expect: on application of the informant or the defendant, vary the conditions

items.title: Peace bond to protect children from sexual offences
items.says: Any person who fears on reasonable grounds that someone will commit a listed sexual offence against a person under 18 may lay an information before a provincial court judge. The bond can last up to 12 months, or up to two years if the defendant has a prior sexual offence against a child.

source.expect: in respect of one or more persons who are under the age of 18 years

items.title: Peace bond for fear of a serious personal injury offence
items.says: A person who fears on reasonable grounds that another will commit a serious personal injury offence may, with the Attorney General's consent, lay an information before a provincial court judge. The bond can last up to 12 months, or two years with a prior conviction for such an offence.

source.expect: with the consent of the Attorney General, lay an information

items.title: Breaching a peace bond
items.says: A person who breaches a recognizance under ss. 810 to 810.2 commits an offence punishable by up to four years on indictment, or on summary conviction.

source.expect: who commits a breach of the recognizance

items.title: Recognizance (Criminal Code form)
items.says: In the Criminal Code, a recognizance means a recognizance in Form 32 entered into before a judge or justice.

source.expect: means a recognizance in Form 32

review.problem: Section 2 defines a recognizance as one in Form 32 entered into before a judge or justice; it does not mention peace bonds or Part XXVIII.

items.title: Family court restraining order (alternative)
items.says: On application, a court may make an interim or final restraining order under the Family Law Act if the applicant has reasonable grounds to fear for their own safety or for the safety of a child in their lawful custody. The order may be made against a spouse or former spouse, or against someone who lives or has lived with the applicant for any period.

source.expect: reasonable grounds to fear for his or her own safety

review.problem: Section 46(2) limits the order to a spouse or former spouse, or a person who is or has been cohabiting with the applicant; 'former partner' wrongly takes in partners who never lived together.

items.title: Criminal proceedings are held in open court
items.says: Criminal proceedings are held in open court, but the judge may exclude the public, or have a witness testify behind a screen, where it is in the interest of the proper administration of justice. Society's interest in encouraging victims to report and take part is a factor.

source.expect: shall be held in open court

items.title: Support person or support animal
items.says: In cases of sexual offences, criminal harassment, trafficking or offences against an intimate partner, the judge must, on application by the prosecutor or the victim-witness, allow a support person or support animal near the witness while testifying, unless it would interfere with the administration of justice.

source.expect: a support person of the witness’s choice or a support animal

items.title: Testifying outside the courtroom or behind a screen
items.says: In the same kinds of cases, the judge must, on application, let a victim-witness testify outside the courtroom or behind a screen so they do not see the accused, unless it would interfere with the proper administration of justice.

source.expect: in respect of a witness who is a victim

items.title: Self-represented accused may not cross-examine the victim
items.says: In sexual offence, criminal harassment, trafficking and intimate partner cases, the judge must, on application by the prosecutor or the victim-witness, order that the accused not personally cross-examine the victim, unless the proper administration of justice requires the accused to do it personally. If the order is made, the judge appoints a lawyer to conduct the cross-examination.

source.expect: Accused not to cross-examine victim

review.problem: Drops the exception that the order is not made where the proper administration of justice requires the accused to cross-examine personally, and the section does not limit it to self-represented accused.

items.title: Court checks that witnesses were told about these aids
items.says: If no application for a support person or support animal is made, the judge must ask the prosecutor whether reasonable steps were taken to tell the witness that one may be made.

source.expect: whether reasonable steps have been taken to inform the witness

review.problem: Section 486.1(1.2) covers only support person or support animal applications; the matching inquiry for testifying outside the courtroom or behind a screen is in s. 486.2, a different section.

items.title: Not disclosing a witness's identity in the proceedings
items.says: On application, the judge may order that information that could identify a witness not be disclosed during the proceedings, where that is in the interest of the proper administration of justice. The hearing may be in private.

source.expect: any information that could identify the witness not be disclosed

items.title: Mandatory publication ban in sexual offence cases
items.says: In proceedings for listed sexual and related offences, the judge must tell the victim (and witnesses under 18) of the right to apply for a ban on publishing identifying information, and must make the order on application by the victim, prosecutor or witness.

source.expect: inform any witness under the age of 18 years and the victim of the right

items.title: Discretionary publication ban for other victims and witnesses
items.says: For other offences, a victim or witness (or the prosecutor) may apply for a ban on publishing information that could identify them, where the judge finds it is in the interest of the proper administration of justice.

source.expect: any information that could identify the victim or witness shall not be published

items.title: Other orders to protect a witness's security
items.says: On application by the prosecutor or a witness, the judge may make any other order needed to protect a witness's security, if it is in the interest of the proper administration of justice.

source.expect: necessary to protect the security of any witness

items.title: Protecting a complainant's private records
items.says: In sexual offence cases, when the accused seeks a complainant's private records held by someone else, the judge holds a hearing in private. The complainant may appear and make submissions, cannot be compelled to testify there, has the right to a lawyer, and cannot be ordered to pay costs.

source.expect: may appear and make submissions at the hearing

items.title: Victims told about plea agreements
items.says: For murder, serious personal injury offences and other indictable offences with a maximum of five years or more, the court asks whether victims were told about a plea agreement. If a victim was not told before the plea was accepted, the prosecutor must take reasonable steps to tell them as soon as feasible. The plea stays valid either way.

source.expect: take reasonable steps to inform the victim of the agreement

items.title: Victim impact statement
items.says: When sentencing, the court must consider any statement a victim prepared and filed describing the physical or emotional harm, property damage or economic loss caused by the offence and its impact on them.

source.expect: the court shall consider any statement of a victim

items.title: Court asks whether the victim had the chance
items.says: After a finding of guilt and before sentence, the court must ask the prosecutor whether reasonable steps were taken to give the victim an opportunity to prepare a statement.

source.expect: the court shall inquire of the prosecutor if reasonable steps have been taken

items.title: Adjournment to prepare a statement
items.says: On application of the prosecutor or the victim, or on its own, the court may adjourn so the victim can prepare a statement or present evidence, if this would not interfere with the proper administration of justice.

source.expect: On application of the prosecutor or a victim

items.title: Form 34.2: Victim Impact Statement
items.says: The statement is prepared in writing on Form 34.2, following the procedures of the program the province has designated for that purpose.

source.expect: using Form 34.2 in Part XXVIII

review.problem: Section 722(4) does not name Ontario's Victim/Witness Assistance Program or say that it helps with the form.

items.title: How the statement can be presented
items.says: On the victim's request, the court must let them read the statement, read it with a support person or support animal nearby, read it outside the courtroom or behind a screen, or present it another appropriate way. The victim may have a photo of themselves from before the offence.

source.expect: permit the victim to present the statement

items.title: Only relevant parts are considered
items.says: In considering a victim impact statement, the court takes into account the parts it considers relevant to the sentence (or to a discharge) and disregards the rest.

source.expect: disregard any other portion

review.problem: Section 722(8) covers only which parts of the statement the court considers; giving a copy to the offender and prosecutor is in s. 722.1, a different section.

items.title: Copy of the statement to the offender
items.says: The court clerk provides a copy of the victim impact statement to the offender or their lawyer, and to the prosecutor, as soon as practicable after a finding of guilt.

source.expect: provide a copy of a statement referred to in subsection 722(1)

items.title: Community impact statement
items.says: A person may also file, on Form 34.3, a statement on a community's behalf describing harm or loss to the community, which the court must consider at sentencing.

source.expect: any statement made by an individual on a community’s behalf

items.title: Victim statement at a Review Board or NCR disposition hearing
items.says: Where an accused is found not criminally responsible or unfit, a victim may file a written statement (Form 48.2) with the court or Review Board describing the harm and the offence's impact.

source.expect: A victim of the offence may prepare and file with the court or Review Board

items.title: No-contact order during a jail sentence
items.says: A sentencing judge may order the offender not to communicate with any victim, witness or other named person while in custody. Breaking the order is an offence.

source.expect: during the custodial period of the sentence

items.title: No-contact condition in probation
items.says: A probation order may require the offender not to communicate with any victim, witness or other named person, or go to named places.

source.expect: abstain from communicating, directly or indirectly, with any victim

items.title: Victim surcharge
items.says: An offender convicted or discharged must pay a victim surcharge for each offence: 30% of any fine, or $100 (summary) or $200 (indictable) if there is no fine. The court can waive or reduce it for undue hardship or disproportion. The money is used to help victims.

source.expect: shall pay a victim surcharge for each offence

items.title: Court must consider restitution
items.says: When an offender is convicted or discharged, the sentencing court must consider making a restitution order.

source.expect: shall consider making a restitution order under section 738 or 739

items.title: Court asks whether victims were asked about restitution
items.says: After a finding of guilt and before sentence, the court must ask the prosecutor whether victims were given an opportunity to say whether they seek restitution for losses that are readily ascertainable. The court may adjourn so victims can do so.

source.expect: an opportunity to indicate whether they are seeking restitution

items.title: Form 34.1: Statement on Restitution
items.says: A victim may say they are seeking restitution using Form 34.1 or another approved form or method, and must establish their losses, the amount of which must be readily ascertainable.

source.expect: by completing Form 34.1 in Part XXVIII

items.title: Reasons if restitution is not ordered
items.says: If a victim seeks restitution and the court does not order it, the court must give reasons on the record.

source.expect: shall include in the record a statement of the court’s reasons

items.title: Restitution for property loss or damage
items.says: For damage to or loss of property, the court may order payment up to the replacement value of the property, less the value of any part returned, if the amount is readily ascertainable.

source.expect: an amount not exceeding the replacement value of the property

items.title: Restitution for bodily or psychological harm
items.says: For bodily or psychological harm caused by the offence, the court may order payment of up to all pecuniary (money) damages caused by the harm, including lost income or support, if the amount is readily ascertainable.

source.expect: including loss of income or support, if the amount is readily ascertainable

review.problem: Section 738(1)(b) says nothing about pain and suffering or about a civil claim for it.

items.title: Restitution for household members harmed or threatened
items.says: Where the offender's intimate partner, child or another household member suffered or was threatened with harm, the court may order the offender to pay reasonable expenses of moving out, temporary housing, food, child care and transportation, if readily ascertainable.

source.expect: was a member of the offender’s household at the relevant time

items.title: Restitution for identity theft and intimate image removal
items.says: For identity theft or fraud, restitution can cover reasonable costs to re-establish identity and correct credit history. For sharing an intimate image without consent, it can cover reasonable costs to remove the image from the internet.

source.expect: incurs expenses to remove the intimate image from the Internet

items.title: Restitution to good-faith purchasers
items.says: Where stolen property was sold to or used as loan security with a person acting in good faith and the property was returned to its owner, the court may order the offender to repay that person.

source.expect: to a person acting in good faith and without notice

items.title: Ability to pay does not prevent restitution
items.says: The offender's financial means or ability to pay does not stop the court from making a restitution order.

source.expect: does not prevent the court from making an order

items.title: Payment date or instalments
items.says: A restitution order must require payment of the full amount by a set day, unless the court decides on payment by instalments, in which case the order sets out a payment schedule.

source.expect: pay the full amount specified in the order by the day specified

review.problem: Naming several people with amounts and priority is in s. 739.3, not s. 739.2.

items.title: Order payable through a public authority
items.says: At the victim's request, the court may make the order in favour of a designated public authority, which enforces it and passes payments to the victim.

source.expect: in favour of a public authority, designated by the regulations

items.title: Restitution comes before fines and forfeiture
items.says: Where the offender cannot pay both restitution and a fine, or property could be forfeited, the court makes the restitution order first and then considers the fine or forfeiture.

source.expect: the court shall first make the order of restitution

items.title: Unpaid probation payments continue as restitution
items.says: If a probation or conditional sentence order requiring payment ends before everything is paid, the payment requirement continues as a restitution order until paid.

source.expect: deemed to continue as a restitution order

items.title: Victim gets notice of the restitution order
items.says: The court must give the person to be paid a notice of the content of the restitution order, or a copy of it.

source.expect: cause notice of the content of the order

items.title: Filing an unpaid restitution order as a civil judgment
items.says: If the offender misses the payment date or an instalment, the person owed may file the order in any civil court with jurisdiction for the amount and enter the unpaid amount as a judgment, enforceable like any civil judgment.

source.expect: enter as a judgment any amount ordered to be paid that remains unpaid

items.title: Money found on the offender at arrest
items.says: The court may direct that restitution be paid from money found on the offender when arrested, if no one else disputes ownership of it.

source.expect: taken out of moneys found in the possession of the offender

items.title: Enforcing in Small Claims Court: garnishment
items.says: In Small Claims Court, a creditor may enforce an order for the payment of money by garnishment of debts that other people owe to the debtor.

source.expect: by garnishment of debts payable to the debtor

review.problem: Rule 20.08(1) says only that an order for payment may be enforced by garnishing debts owed to the debtor by others; it does not mention entering a restitution order as a judgment or name wages or bank accounts.

items.title: Restitution does not bar a civil lawsuit
items.says: A restitution order does not, by itself, affect any civil remedy the victim has for the same act.

source.expect: A civil remedy for an act or omission is not affected

items.title: Notification of release from an Ontario jail
items.says: Ontario's principles call for notifying victims of prescribed crimes, on request, of an offender's release (including temporary absence and parole) and of any escape, and for Review Board notifications where an accused is found unfit or not criminally responsible.

source.expect: any hearing held with respect to the accused by the Review Board

items.title: Information from federal corrections
items.says: For offenders serving two years or more, a registered victim may request information from the Correctional Service of Canada and Parole Board of Canada, including release dates and conditions, and may present a victim statement at parole hearings.

source.citation: Corrections and Conditional Release Act, S.C. 1992, c. 20
source.expect: at the request of a victim

items.title: Getting a copy of an Ontario Court of Justice recording
items.says: Members of the public and self-represented parties can get a copy of a digital audio recording of an OCJ proceeding only with a court order, after completing the request form and undertaking and paying the copy fee. The order is sought from the presiding judicial officer or, if unavailable, the regional or local administrative judge or justice.

source.expect: with a court order and upon completion of the appropriate court request form

items.title: OCJ recordings that are not available
items.says: Unless a judicial officer orders otherwise, there is no access to OCJ recordings of in camera or closed proceedings, proceedings with restrictions on records, Youth Criminal Justice Act proceedings, and case, settlement and trial management conferences.

source.expect: Proceedings under the Youth Criminal Justice Act

items.title: Court files, documents and exhibits
items.says: Court records are managed by the Ministry of the Attorney General. Requests to see a court file are made at the court location where the matter was heard, under the Ministry's access policy. Some youth and other criminal records may not be available.

source.expect: should be made at the court location where the matter was heard

items.title: Ordering a transcript
items.says: Court transcripts are certified written records of a hearing, prepared by Authorized Court Transcriptionists. Unless a judge orders otherwise, transcripts are not available for case, settlement and trial management conferences.

source.expect: are a certified written record of a court hearing

items.title: Superior Court recordings for members of the public
items.says: Unless a Superior Court judge orders otherwise, members of the public are not given digital recordings of court proceedings. They may request access by seeking a court order using the Request/Undertaking Form and paying the prescribed fee; a person under an order made under s. 140 of the Courts of Justice Act must first get a judge's leave.

source.pinpoint: Access to Digital Recordings for Members of the Public
source.expect: members of the public will not be provided access to digital recordings

review.problem: The policy does not mention victims, and it leaves out that a person under a vexatious-litigant order (CJA s. 140) must first get leave.

items.title: Recordings are not the official record
items.says: Digital recordings are not an official court record and cannot be used for appeal purposes; access is at the court's discretion and subject to publication bans.

source.expect: are not considered an official court record

items.title: No recording or broadcasting of court audio
items.says: No one may take a photograph or audio recording at a court hearing, or broadcast or reproduce one, except as the Courts of Justice Act allows. Breaking this rule is an offence.

source.expect: take or attempt to take a photograph

items.title: Civil court documents are public
items.says: On paying the fee, anyone may see a document filed in a civil proceeding, unless a law or court order says otherwise. A court may seal documents.

source.expect: is entitled to see any document filed in a civil proceeding

items.title: Crown Attorney acts for the Attorney General
items.says: Every Crown Attorney and every provincial prosecutor is the agent of the Attorney General for the purposes of the Criminal Code.

source.expect: Attorney-General’s agent

review.problem: Section 10 does not say that the Crown represents the public rather than the victim or that the victim is not the Crown's client.

items.title: Crown Attorney duties in prosecutions
items.says: A Crown Attorney examines the charges and papers sent by justices, may cause charges to be further investigated so prosecutions are not delayed or fail for want of proof, and conducts prosecutions of indictable offences.

source.expect: cause such charges to be further investigated

items.title: Who can be sued over a prosecution
items.says: A person who was prosecuted cannot sue a Crown Attorney personally for things done in the prosecution; the action is brought against the Attorney General instead, who stands in the Crown Attorney's place.

source.expect: may be commenced against the Attorney General

items.title: Krieger v. Law Society of Alberta
items.says: The Supreme Court of Canada described prosecutorial discretion, including decisions to start, continue or stay a prosecution, and held that courts and others generally do not review these core decisions except for abuse of process.

source.decision: Krieger v. Law Society of Alberta, 2002 SCC 65

items.title: Nelles v. Ontario
items.says: The Supreme Court of Canada held that Crown prosecutors do not have absolute immunity from a lawsuit for malicious prosecution, while the Crown itself was immune under the law then in force.

source.expect: absolute immunity from a suit for malicious prosecution

items.title: Miazga v. Kvello Estate
items.says: The Supreme Court of Canada set out the elements of malicious prosecution against a Crown prosecutor, including absence of reasonable and probable cause and malice in the sense of an improper purpose.

source.expect: absence of reasonable and probable cause

items.title: Henry v. British Columbia (Attorney General)
items.says: The Supreme Court of Canada held that Charter damages may be awarded against the Crown for wrongful non-disclosure by prosecutors, where the claimant meets the fault standard the Court set out.

source.decision: Henry v. British Columbia (Attorney General), 2015 SCC 24
source.expect: Wrongful non-disclosure

items.title: Complaint about police conduct (LECA)
items.says: Any person, other than those listed in subsection (2) (such as members of the same police service), may make a complaint to the Complaints Director about the conduct of a police officer or other person covered by section 152 of the Act.

source.expect: Any person may make a complaint to the Complaints Director

review.problem: Section 154(1) does not name the Law Enforcement Complaints Agency, covers the conduct of any person referred to in s. 152 (not only police officers), and is subject to the restrictions in subsection (2).

items.title: Complaint made elsewhere is forwarded
items.says: If the complaint is made instead to a chief of police, police service board, the Minister or others listed, they must forward it to the Complaints Director and tell the complainant.

source.expect: shall forward the complaint to the Complaints Director

items.title: Complaints Director reviews the complaint
items.says: The Complaints Director reviews every complaint, decides whether it is about the conduct of a person covered by the Act, and if so causes it to be investigated, subject to the power to refuse.

source.expect: cause the complaint to be investigated

items.title: Six-month window for police complaints
items.says: The Complaints Director may refuse to investigate if the facts happened more than six months before the complaint, considering whether the complainant was a minor or had a disability, was subject to a criminal proceeding about the events, and the public interest. A complaint can also be refused if the complainant was not affected by the conduct.

source.expect: occurred more than six months before the complaint is made

items.title: Who counts as affected by police conduct
items.says: Only a person the conduct was directed at, a person who saw or heard it while physically present, or a person in a personal relationship with the first who suffered loss, damage, distress, danger or inconvenience is considered affected.

source.expect: A person at whom the conduct was directed

items.title: Special Investigations Unit
items.says: The Special Investigations Unit investigates incidents where police or other officials may have caused a death, serious injury, sexual assault or firearm discharge at a person through criminal conduct.

source.citation: Special Investigations Unit Act, 2019, S.O. 2019, c. 1, Sched. 5
source.expect: The death of a person

items.title: Hill v. Hamilton-Wentworth Regional Police Services Board
items.says: The Supreme Court of Canada recognized the tort of negligent investigation: police owe a duty of care to a suspect being investigated, judged against the standard of a reasonable officer.

source.decision: Hill v. Hamilton-Wentworth Regional Police Services Board, 2007 SCC 41
source.expect: tort of negligent investigation

items.title: Suing the offender in Small Claims Court
items.says: A Small Claims Court action is started by filing a Plaintiff's Claim (Form 7A) with the clerk, with a copy for each defendant (no copies are needed if the claim is filed electronically).

source.expect: filing a plaintiff's claim (Form 7A)

review.problem: Rule 7.01(1) says only how an action is started; it says nothing about victims suing or the $50,000 limit.

items.title: Small Claims Court limit
items.says: The Small Claims Court hears claims for money or property up to $50,000.

items.title: Suing the offender in the Superior Court
items.says: In the Superior Court of Justice, an action is usually started by a statement of claim (Form 14A), or by a notice of action (Form 14C) where there is not enough time to prepare a statement of claim.

source.expect: is a statement of claim (Form 14A

review.problem: Rule 14.03(1) does not say which claims are 'larger' or tie the statement of claim to claim size; it also lists exceptions such as a notice of action.

items.title: Two-year basic limitation period
items.says: Unless the Act says otherwise, a lawsuit must start within two years of the day the claim was discovered.

source.expect: after the second anniversary of the day on which the claim was discovered

items.title: When a claim is discovered
items.says: A claim is discovered on the earlier of the day the person knew, or a reasonable person in their circumstances ought to have known, that the harm happened, was caused by an act or omission of the person to be sued, and that a lawsuit would be an appropriate way to remedy it. The person is presumed to know on the day of the act unless shown otherwise.

source.expect: the day on which the person with the claim first knew

items.title: Limitation period paused for minors
items.says: The two-year period does not run while the person with the claim is a minor and not represented by a litigation guardian.

source.expect: is a minor

items.title: Limitation period paused for incapable persons
items.says: The two-year period does not run while the person is incapable of starting a lawsuit because of their physical, mental or psychological condition and has no litigation guardian. Capacity is presumed unless shown otherwise.

source.expect: because of his or her physical, mental or psychological condition

items.title: 15-year ultimate limitation period
items.says: No lawsuit may be started more than 15 years after the act or omission, subject to the Act's exceptions.

source.expect: 15th anniversary of the day on which the act or omission

items.title: No limitation period for sexual assault claims
items.says: There is no limitation period for a lawsuit based on a sexual assault.

source.expect: a proceeding based on a sexual assault

items.title: No limitation period: other sexual misconduct
items.says: There is no limitation period for a lawsuit based on other misconduct of a sexual nature if the person was a minor, or the other person had charge of them, was in a position of trust or authority, or the person was dependent on them.

source.expect: any other misconduct of a sexual nature

items.title: No limitation period: assault by an intimate partner or on a minor
items.says: There is no limitation period for a lawsuit based on an assault if the person was a minor at the time, or the two had an intimate relationship, or the person was dependent on the assailant.

source.expect: they had an intimate relationship

items.title: These exceptions apply to old events
items.says: The no-limitation rules for sexual assault, sexual misconduct and these assaults apply whenever the act happened, even if an earlier limitation period had expired, unless the case was already dismissed with no appeal left or settled.

source.expect: regardless of the expiry of any previously applicable limitation period

items.title: All related claims are covered
items.says: The no-limitation rules extend to all claims in the lawsuit about that act, including negligence, breach of fiduciary or other duty, and vicarious liability (for example against an employer or institution).

source.expect: for breach of fiduciary or any other duty or for vicarious liability

items.title: Battery and sexual battery: what must be shown
items.says: Battery is intentional, direct, harmful or offensive physical contact. In a sexual battery claim, the plaintiff proves the sexual contact; if the defendant does not dispute it happened, the defendant bears the burden of proving consent or that a reasonable person would have thought there was consent.

source.decision: Non-Marine Underwriters, Lloyd's of London v. Scalera, 2000 SCC 24
source.expect: he bears the burden of proving that the plaintiff consented

items.title: Intentional infliction of mental suffering
items.says: To claim for intentional infliction of mental suffering, the plaintiff shows conduct that was flagrant and outrageous, calculated to produce harm, and that resulted in a visible and provable illness.

source.decision: Prinzo v. Baycrest Centre for Geriatric Care (2002), 60 O.R. (3d) 474 (C.A.)
source.expect: flagrant and outrageous

items.title: Proving mental injury
items.says: A claimant does not need a diagnosed psychiatric illness to recover for mental injury in negligence; the injury must be serious and prolonged and more than ordinary upset.

source.expect: recognized psychiatric illness

items.title: A conviction is proof in the civil case
items.says: Proof that a person was convicted or discharged of a crime anywhere in Canada is proof, unless there is evidence to the contrary, that they committed it, once appeals are finished or the time to appeal has passed.

source.expect: is proof, in the absence of evidence to the contrary

items.title: Damages for emotional distress after a prescribed crime
items.says: A person convicted of a prescribed crime is liable to every victim for emotional distress, and bodily harm resulting from the distress, arising from the crime.

source.expect: liable in damages to every victim of the crime for emotional distress

items.title: Presumed emotional distress
items.says: For a prescribed crime, certain victims are presumed to have suffered emotional distress, including victims of sexual assault or attempted sexual assault, other sexual crimes, assault by a spouse, non-consensual sharing of intimate images, human trafficking, and assault on a minor or person with a disability by someone in a position of trust or on whom they were dependent.

source.expect: shall be presumed to have suffered emotional distress

items.title: Prescribed crimes regulation
items.says: The crimes to which the Ontario damages and notification provisions apply are listed in a regulation made under the Act.

source.citation: O. Reg. 456/96 (Prescribed Crimes) under the Victims' Bill of Rights, 1995
source.expect: prescribed crimes

items.title: Limits on security for costs against a victim
items.says: In a victim's lawsuit against the person convicted of the crime, a judge does not order the victim to pay security for costs unless, considering the spirit and purpose of the Act, it is necessary in the interests of justice.

source.expect: requiring a victim to provide security for costs

items.title: The criminal sentence and damages
items.says: When ordering the convicted person to pay damages, the judge does not consider the criminal sentence, except that the sentence is taken into account before ordering punitive damages.

source.expect: shall not consider the sentence

items.title: Interest on a victim's award
items.says: A judge does not disallow interest on a victim's award under the Courts of Justice Act unless necessary in the interests of justice.

source.expect: to disallow an award of interest to a victim

items.title: Costs on a solicitor and client basis
items.says: A judge who awards costs to a victim makes the order on a solicitor and client (higher) basis, unless that would not be in the interests of justice.

source.expect: shall make the order on a solicitor and client basis

items.title: Offer to settle
items.says: In Small Claims Court, a party may serve on any other party an offer to settle the claim on the terms set out in the offer.

source.expect: an offer to settle a claim on the terms specified in the offer

review.problem: Rule 14.01 does not say an offer may be made 'at any time'; that is in r. 14.02(1), a separate rule.

items.title: Forfeited proceeds of crime and victim compensation
items.says: Under Ontario's Civil Remedies Act, 2001, the Attorney General can ask the Superior Court to forfeit property that is proceeds of unlawful activity; money from forfeited property can be used to compensate persons who suffered losses from that activity.

source.expect: compensate persons who suffered pecuniary or non-pecuniary losses

items.title: Suing the Crown or police over how the case was handled
items.says: A lawsuit that includes a claim for damages cannot be brought against the Ontario Crown unless, at least 60 days before it starts, the claimant serves on the Crown a notice of the claim with enough details to identify the occasion it arose from.

source.expect: at least 60 days before the commencement of the proceeding

review.problem: Section 18(1) covers only the 60-day notice; the leave requirement for misfeasance or bad-faith claims is in s. 17, and the cross-reference to another area is not law.

items.title: Leave needed for misfeasance or bad-faith claims against the Crown
items.says: A lawsuit against the Crown or a Crown employee for misfeasance in public office or a bad-faith tort may proceed only with the court's leave, and is stayed until leave is granted.

source.expect: may proceed only with leave of the court

items.title: Victim/Witness Assistance Program
items.says: Ontario's Victim/Witness Assistance Program gives information, assistance and support to victims and witnesses throughout the criminal court process.

source.expect: provides information, assistance and support to victims and witnesses

items.title: Victim Support Line
items.says: The Victim Support Line offers 24/7 information and referrals for victims of crime across Ontario: 1-888-579-2888.

source.expect: information and referrals for victims of crime across Ontario

items.title: Victim Crisis Assistance Ontario
items.says: Victim Crisis Assistance Ontario provides 24/7 crisis intervention, safety planning, referrals, and help applying to the Victim Quick Response Program+.

source.expect: provides crisis intervention services to victims of crime

items.title: Victim Quick Response Program+
items.says: The Victim Quick Response Program+ gives short-term support for essential expenses right after a violent crime (such as emergency home safety, counselling, crime-scene clean-up and funeral costs) to people with no other means. Applicants are assessed by a local service provider.

source.expect: short-term support for essential expenses for victims

items.title: Vulnerable Victims and Family Fund
items.says: This fund helps victims take part in the criminal court process, for example with travel to key court dates, interpretation and disability accommodations. Victims apply through the Victim/Witness Assistance Program.

source.expect: helps victims of crime participate more fully in the criminal court process

items.title: Free independent legal advice for sexual assault survivors
items.says: Sexual assault survivors living in Ontario may be eligible for up to 4 hours of free, confidential legal advice by phone or video. It does not include representation in court.

source.expect: up to 4 hours of free legal advice

items.title: Child Victim/Witness Program
items.says: The Child Victim/Witness Program supports child victims and witnesses during the criminal court process.

source.pinpoint: Help for child victims and child witnesses
source.expect: offers support and services to child victims and witnesses

items.title: R. v. Antic
items.says: The Supreme Court of Canada set out principles for contested bail hearings, including the ladder principle: release is favoured at the earliest reasonable opportunity on the least onerous grounds, and each more onerous form of release must be justified.

source.expect: the following principles and guidelines should be adhered to

items.title: R. v. Zora
items.says: The Supreme Court of Canada held that bail conditions must be clearly stated, minimal in number, necessary, reasonable, least onerous, and linked to the risks under the detention grounds (restraint and review), and that the breach offence requires proof of subjective fault.

source.expect: the principles of restraint and review

items.title: R. v. St-Cloud
items.says: The Supreme Court of Canada held that the third ground (confidence in the administration of justice) is a distinct ground for detention, not limited to rare cases, and that the court weighs all the circumstances without ordering detention automatically.

source.expect: does not create a residual ground for detention

items.title: R. v. Myers
items.says: The Supreme Court of Canada explained the 90-day detention review: the judge asks whether continued detention is still justified on the grounds in s. 515(10), and considers any unreasonable delay.

source.expect: Pre-trial detention is the exception, not the rule

items.title: R. v. Morales
items.says: The Supreme Court of Canada held that the Charter right not to be denied reasonable bail without just cause allows denial of bail only in a narrow set of circumstances where necessary for the proper functioning of the bail system.

source.expect: just cause

items.title: R. v. Hall
items.says: The Supreme Court of Canada upheld detention to maintain confidence in the administration of justice, while striking down a broader 'any other just cause' ground.

source.expect: confidence in the administration of justice

items.title: R. v. Jordan
items.says: The Supreme Court of Canada set presumptive ceilings for the time from charge to the end of trial (18 months in provincial court, 30 months in superior court), beyond which delay is presumed unreasonable and the charge may be stayed.

items.title: R. v. J.J.
items.says: The Supreme Court of Canada upheld the Criminal Code regime for admitting a complainant's private records held by the accused in sexual offence cases, including the complainant's right to participate in the hearing.
